prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at the magic wavelength brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock (B027) with Katori and Ye as a single-part prize. Having read all eight round-1 statements and the chair's questions, my reasons are sharper than in round 1. The discovery is the magic-wavelength lattice: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shift cancels between the two clock levels, and thousands of neutral atoms can be held tightly enough to remove Doppler and recoil shifts while the atom number stays large. That is a new way to combine a narrow transition with a large ensemble, and it is not the comb (2005) or single-ion control (2012) applied to a new species. Those prizes made the tools available. This scheme is a different physical route to the same goal. The claim has been tested the way an instrument builder wants it tested: independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) build lattice clocks, compare them and agree near 1e-18, and the same clocks have already seen gravitational redshift over millimetres and tightened bounds on constants. On the chair's question about timing, I do not think the committee should wait for the CGPM to redefine the second. The prize would be for the invention and its demonstrated performance, and the redefinition is a consequence that depends on metrology politics and not on the physics. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist and leaves the three-person limit unused, so nothing forces an arbitrary cut.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real and the citation has to be written so that it rests on the lattice clock itself. For that reason I prefer wording that names the magic-wavelength trapping and the 1e-18 level, in line with Danielsson's point that it should not read as a third award for better clocks. The fundamental content so far is tighter bounds and redshift tests, not a surprise from nature, as Lindroth and Danielsson both note, so a reader could call this a measurement capability and not a discovery. Credit is not perfectly closed: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Oates have claims on parts of the development, and Olsson's question whether Ye is originator or developer of the concept is fair. My own answer is that Katori is the originator of the lattice and magic-wavelength scheme and Ye is the one who made it a record-accuracy clock and opened the many-body regime, which is a decisive development and justifies the second name, but I accept that others may weigh Ye's role differently. Finally, I am an instrument builder and judge this case with more confidence than condensed-matter alternatives.

responses.point: Eriksson holds B057 first and argues that the 2016 prize covered topological phases in model systems, whereas B057 concerns time-reversal-invariant band insulators in real materials, and that the Kane-Mele proposal and Molenkamp's measurement form a defensible core. He also says he would not object strongly if the committee preferred B027.
responses.response: I accept his distinction from 2016 and I rate the verification as strong: decades of transport and ARPES results, and a theory that predicts the measured band structure. That moves B057 up in my alternatives, ahead of the microscope. What keeps it second for me is the credit chain he sets out himself: Kane and Mele in 2005, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang in 2006, and Molenkamp's experiment in 2007. The measured system was the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction, Zhang has died, and the 3D work is outside the trio. A citation can be worded around the proposal and the first observation, but I cannot judge as an outsider whether that reading would hold. If he or Mehlig can state a citation that is true to the sequence without the missing names, I would reconsider. Without that, the clock has the cleaner credit, and he himself says the clock would not be harmed by his choice.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B057 after the openings as the one entry combining a model-level theoretical idea with a quantitative experimental realisation, and states plainly that the 2016 overlap and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap make its attribution less crisp than B027 and its timing weaker.
responses.response: I note that he sets out the weaknesses of his own first choice, and that he keeps B027 as an alternative. Where I differ is on weighing: the theory-plus-experiment arc he values is also present in B027, since Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice clock are followed by Ye's accuracy and many-body work, and there is no credit gap there. I also agree with him that the committee has to say what the Z2 step adds to 2016. I would ask him the question the chair posed: what would move him to B027? I think the two-name credit with independent reproduction should count for him, since his arguments about attribution apply more heavily to his own entry than to mine.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B027 and asks that the citation rest on what the precision has shown (redshift tests, many-body clock physics) so that it does not read as a third award for better clocks after 2005 and 2012. He keeps IceCube (B041) and B057 as alternatives and argues against Higgs and B053 on physics content and credit.
responses.response: I take his wording point and have changed my citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 level, which are the physics, and I would accept adding the redshift and many-body results if colleagues want them. On IceCube I still hold it as my second alternative: it is a new window, but the credited pair stands for the leadership of a collaboration of hundreds, and source identification is incomplete. We agree that the Higgs and the microscope are not practical options this year, although I put the microscope's case on credit (Krivanek) and discipline more than on its physics, since I regard sub-angstrom imaging as a real advance in measurement.

responses.point: Olsson moved to B027 from her own field's B053 and asks whether Ye is the originator or the developer of Katori's concept, and whether the citation should reflect that, while noting that the redefinition of the second has not happened.
responses.response: I respect that she set aside her own field's candidate under a strict standard, and I share her concern about the Krivanek question for B053. On Ye, my reading is that Katori holds the concept and the first strontium lattice clock, while Ye made it a record-accuracy clock and went on to many-body physics in the lattice, so the second name rests on decisive development, not on priority of the idea. I do not think the citation needs to split the two roles, because 'invention and development' covers both, but if the committee wishes to be explicit it can word the citation around the lattice scheme and the accuracy it brought. On timing I think we should act and not wait for the redefinition.

responses.point: Johansson calls the overlap with 2005 and 2012 the deciding issue for B027 and argues that neither prize covers neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice. He also says he would not widen the credit to Zoller or others, since that would blur a clean pair.
responses.response: I agree that this is the deciding issue and I agree with his answer. The 2005 and 2012 prizes made precise frequency measurement and single-quantum-system control possible, but neither covers trapping an ensemble of neutral atoms in a lattice with cancelled light shifts, which is the step that took stability and accuracy to a new regime. I also withdraw the loose suggestion in my first statement that a third name could be added from the early proposal or other clock groups. The committee has no stronger candidate for a third name than the ones the colleagues named, and the clean pair is the better credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a distinct invention from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which Johansson calls the deciding issue.
Whether a credit for Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow or Oates should have been added, and whether Ye's role is read as originator or decisive developer.
Whether the Z2 band-topology credit in B057 can be worded to be true to the sequence of Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Molenkamp, which would make B057 a serious rival.
Whether acting before the redefinition of the second costs anything in the committee's eyes.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. None of the credited names in B027 are at KTH or in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT or XL-Calibur collaborations. I have no tie to B057 or B041 either. As Chair I have tried to hold my own view separate from the process, and I note that my expertise is in astroparticle physics and detectors, so I rely on colleagues for condensed-matter and atomic-theory judgments.
